title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[
\operatorname{NCP}_2\notin\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\forall D\in\mathrm{PPT}\ \forall c>0\ \exists n_0\ge9\ \forall n\ge n_0:
\quad n\text{ a square}\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Adv}_D(n)<n^{-c}.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is the unrestricted binary Nearest Codeword decision problem defined below. The distinguisher receives either \((A,As+e)\) or \((A,u)\), with a uniform \(n^2\times n\) binary matrix, independent uniform secret and comparison vector, and independent noise bits of probability \(1/\sqrt n\). The conclusion requires negligible advantage at all sufficiently large square dimensions for every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher.
why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The primary work obtains low-noise LPN hardness from a simultaneous decoding/dual-code distinguishing assumption and identifies removing that extra foundation as a future direction.
Revision 1 retains that distinction. Its decoder also handles random noise in the stated reduction, rather than supplying a decider for arbitrary Nearest Codeword inputs.

context_blocks.text: LPN averages over the matrix and independent noise, while Nearest Codeword allows an arbitrary matrix and target. Transferring the latter difficulty to the former would connect a worst-case decision assumption with an average-case cryptographic problem.
The new reduction offers a choice: decode the code from random noise or distinguish noisy dual-code structure. Removing the second branch is a substantive additional demand.

The card asks for standard negligible distinguishing advantage throughout all sufficiently large square dimensions. Success confined to an unbounded sparse sequence of dimensions must also be ruled out.

definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo two. For a binary vector \(v\), its Hamming weight \(\operatorname{wt}(v)\) is the number of its one coordinates. An instance of \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is an explicitly given binary matrix \(G\in\mathbb F_2^{a\times b}\), a binary vector \(y\in\mathbb F_2^a\) and an integer \(t\) with \(0\le t\le a\), where \(a,b\ge1\). It is a YES instance exactly when some \(z\in\mathbb F_2^b\) has \(\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t\). The input lists the dimensions, entries and threshold with delimiters, using binary integers and row-major matrix entries. Invalid encodings are NO instances. There is no rank, balance, noise-distribution or closeness promise, and the task asks for one decision bit, not a codeword.

A language is in BPP if a single probabilistic Turing machine halts within a polynomial in the total binary input length on every input and every random tape, and answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. Its fair random bits are private; no advice or oracle is supplied. The premise means that no such machine decides this entire Nearest Codeword language.

For the average-case experiments let \(n=q^2\) with an integer \(q\ge3\). Independently draw all entries of \(A\), all bits of \(s\), and all bits of \(u\) uniformly. In the noisy experiment draw \(e_1,\ldots,e_{n^2}\) independently with \(\Pr[e_i=1]=1/q\), also independently of \(A,s,u\). The noisy vector is \(As+e\), computed over \(\mathbb F_2\); the other experiment uses \(u\). The distinguisher receives \(1^n\), the row-major entries of \(A\), and the corresponding vector with fixed delimiters. The sample count is exactly \(n^2\). It receives neither \(s\) nor \(e\), and cannot request extra samples. Square dimensions make the noise probability exactly rational.

A distinguisher \(D\in\mathrm{PPT}\) is one classical probabilistic Turing machine outputting a bit in worst-case polynomial time in the encoded input length, on every random tape. On these inputs that is equivalent to a polynomial in \(n\). Its description is independent of \(n\), and it has no advice, oracle or preprocessing depending on the particular random matrix. The advantage is
\[
\operatorname{Adv}_D(n)=\left|\Pr[D(1^n,A,As+e)=1]-\Pr[D(1^n,A,u)=1]\right|,
\]
where both probabilities include all experiment randomness and the independent internal randomness of \(D\).

The conclusion is eventual negligible advantage along the square dimensions: for each fixed distinguisher and positive exponent there is a threshold beyond which every square dimension satisfies the displayed upper bound. Its failure means that some fixed distinguisher and exponent have inverse-polynomial advantage at arbitrarily large square dimensions. The user explicitly selected this stronger length convention on 18 September 2026. The unrestricted decision premise, exact sample count and exact noise rate remain editorial specifications of the broader source direction, rather than a theorem stated verbatim there.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. An affirmative proof must obtain eventual negligible advantage, including exclusion of a distinguisher that succeeds only on an unbounded subsequence of square dimensions. A sufficient route converts any such nonnegligible distinguisher into a BPP decider for the entire unrestricted Nearest Codeword language. A refutation must establish both the Nearest Codeword premise and a distinguisher violating the conclusion; an oracle separation or failure of a particular reduction is insufficient. An additional dual-code hardness assumption, a different sample/noise regime or only the exclusion of distinguishers successful at every sufficiently large length does not settle this target.

formulation_history.formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[
\operatorname{NCP}_2\notin\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\forall D\in\mathrm{PPT}\ \forall c>0\ \forall n_0\ge1\ \exists n\ge n_0:\
n\text{ is a square},\quad n\ge9,\quad \operatorname{Adv}_D(n)<n^{-c}.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is the binary Nearest Codeword decision problem defined below, and \(D\) distinguishes \((A,As+e)\) from \((A,u)\), where \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}\), the secret \(s\in\mathbb F_2^n\) and \(u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}\) are independent and uniform, and the coordinates of \(e\) are independent with probability \(1/\sqrt n\) of being one. The algorithm is uniform and classical. Equivalently, any polynomial-time distinguisher with inverse-polynomial advantage on every sufficiently large square dimension must imply \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\in\mathrm{BPP}\).
formulation_history.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. A sufficient affirmative solution is a proved transformation taking any distinguisher with the eventual lower bound on advantage to a BPP decider for the stated unrestricted decision problem. A refutation must establish both the Nearest Codeword premise and a distinguisher violating the conclusion; an oracle separation or a limitation of one proposed reduction does not refute the literal unrelativized implication. Adding joint hardness of a dual-code problem, changing the noise rate or sample count, or obtaining hardness only from a more restricted decoding assumption does not settle this target.
